title: Chapter 104 – The Defector
html:
[Gray Peak Mine – Lin Jian]

He wakes to the sound of a pick on stone, and for a long time he cannot remember why that is a comfort.

It rings somewhere above him, a patient steady beat, three strokes and a pause, three strokes and a pause. The air is warm and thick and smells of coal smoke, wet rock, and lamp oil. He lies on his back on something hard and narrow, with a rough wool blanket pulled to his chin, and stares at a ceiling of black stone that glitters faintly in the lamplight, as if the mountain had been sewn with stars.

Gray Peak, he thinks. The mine.

He tries to move his left arm, and the world goes white. It is a clean, total whiteness, the whiteness of a page with nothing written on it, and it lasts so long that he begins to think it will not end.

When it clears, he is breathing in short sobs and sweating through the blanket, and something small and cold has crawled onto his chest and is pressing its snout under his chin.

Awake, says Pebble. Awake. Awake. The voice is a shiver of relief. Three days. Three days sleep. I counted.

"Three days."

Bad. Very bad. Arm gray. Then black. Then less black. A pause. Zhao Bei said bad words. I liked them.

He laughs, or tries to. It comes out as a cough. A wave of weakness goes through him, and he lies back and lets it pass. Slowly he turns his head.

It is a small side-chamber cut in the rock, no bigger than a cell, with a cot, a stool, a clay jug of water, and a lamp hung on a nail. A curtain of sacking hangs across the doorway. Beyond it, he can hear the murmur of voices and the clink of tools and the distant sound of the pick. The wall beside him is scratched with tally marks, hundreds of them, in rows, each row crossed through with a diagonal.

A woman sits on the stool with her back against the wall.

She is broad and scarred and weathered, with gray hair cropped close to her skull and a face the color of old leather. She is whittling something with a short knife. She does not look up.

"The boy in the gray cloak," says Zhao Bei. "I wondered if you would wake."

* * *

She tells him in pieces, over the course of an afternoon, while he drinks broth from a wooden bowl and lies with his back propped against the wall.

She was on the surface, she says, checking the lamp rack at the adit when she saw the lights in the field. Four of them, on the road below. She knows that kind of light. It is the cold blue-gray of a thread-wound dead thing, and she has seen it before in these hills. She went down with a pick and a miner's lamp and a hundred and sixty pounds of old temper.

"I did not know it was you," she says. "I thought it was a traveler. I would have done the same for a goat."

"Thank you."

"Do not thank me. The shadows are still out there. They watch the mine road. They have been watching for two days." She cuts a curl from the whittled stick. "They did not come in. They will not, not while I am in the adit. Twenty years I have been in this hole. The Registry knows what I am."

"And what are you?"

"A very bad neighbor." A flicker of dry humor crosses her scarred face. "I took a pick to a Blood Shadow in my second year. Cracked its skull. They do not like that. They left me alone after."

He looks at her. She is perhaps fifty, but the hands that hold the knife are the hands of a much older woman, thick-knuckled, seamed with coal dust, with three fingers on the left stiff and bent. The shoulder under the miner's jerkin is as wide as a door.

"You are Zhao Heng's sister," he says.

"I am." She sets down the stick. "You have seen him."

"Eight days ago."

She says nothing for a moment. The lamp flickers.

"How is he?"

"Dying," says Jian. "The blood-thread is in his lung. Bai says a year. Perhaps less."

"Ah." The lined face does not change. "He would. He always was a man who did things the hard way." She picks up the knife again. "Twenty years, and he never once came. Not a letter. Not a word. I wrote him in the first year, and the letter came back unopened. After that I stopped." The blade turns in her hands. "I thought he hated me."

"He did not hate you."

"No?"

"He gave me a key and a deed and a letter." Jian chooses his words with care. "He said he wished he had wanted the boy out a year ago. That he had wanted other things."

"That sounds like Heng." Her mouth twists. "Other things. He wanted the family. He wanted the name. He wanted to be the man our father was." She puts the knife down. "I wanted to be a woman who stood in front of a girl when a man was beating her. It cost me twenty years. It was cheap at the price."

The sacking at the door shifts, and she stands.

* * *

She leaves him alone for an hour, and he uses it to take his own measure.

He pulls back the blanket and looks at the arm. It is a terrible thing. From the shoulder to the wrist the skin is the dull color of wet ash, and the veins stand out beneath it in black cords, thick as a quill. The Spring Vein, which once ran green and bright along the inside of the forearm, is a scar now, a seared line from elbow to palm. When he flexes the fingers, they close slowly, as though through mud. When he tries to feel the Qi in the arm, there is a cold place where it should be.

He opens the panel.

```
STATUS — OPERATOR LIN JIAN
Qi: Foundation Early (step 5). Body: step 5. Soul: step 4.
Vital: 61% (recovering). Marrow loss: 7% (permanent unless repaired).
Spring Vein: DAMAGED. Integrity 58%.
Yield now: 0.5 CE per draw. Dormancy pain below freezing.
Self-draw: LOCKED (safety).
Seal: strained (third strain; 21 days to recover).
CE: 3.
Note: bench repair of Spring Vein available at Level 4 (cost: 35 CE).
```

Fifty-eight, he thinks. And half a point a draw. It is a number a clerk would write in a ledger without a flicker, and a man would carry in his arm for the rest of his life.

It is the exact shape of what he has done. A tool, once good, now blunt. A gift paid for with the part of the arm that held it. He reads the line about repair three times. Thirty-five. Thirty-five of the forty he already owes for the soul. He can pay one or the other. Perhaps neither, for a year.

Every advantage has a cost. He has said it so often that it has begun to sound like a prayer. He has never before understood how it feels to be the one who is billed.

Pebble scrambles up onto the pillow and presses its warm flank against his neck.

Not your fault, it says stoutly. You were brave. Brave is expensive.

"That is the first wise thing you have ever said."

I say wise things all the time. A pause. You never listen.

He puts his good hand on the little animal's back, and does not argue.

* * *

Bei returns with the lamp refilled and a flat loaf under her arm.

"Your friend is here," says Bei, without looking round. "I sent a boy to the inn. I thought you would want him."

* * *

The man who steps through the curtain is sixty, thin, and unremarkable in every way, which Jian realizes after a moment is itself remarkable.

He wears a plain brown robe, patched at the knee, and a felt cap. He carries a small leather satchel. His face is long and mild and slightly stooped, with gentle eyes behind a pair of wire-rimmed spectacles, and a gray mustache so neatly trimmed that it might have been drawn on. If Jian had passed him in a market, he would not have remembered him ten steps on. He has the kind of face that is made to be forgotten.

His hands are perfectly still.

"Yan Zhi," says Bei. "Innkeeper. Heng's friend. Do not let him pour you tea. He will talk for an hour."

"I do not talk for an hour," says the man mildly. His voice is dry and soft and precise. "I talk for fifty-three minutes. It is a matter of principle." He bows to Jian, a small accurate bow. "Gate Bearer. I am glad to see you alive. It was a near thing, I am told."

"You know who I am."

"I have known who you are for two years." The mild eyes rest on him without any hurry. "I was a clerk in the Office of the Registry for thirty-one. I wrote your name in a ledger on the day you stood on the forty-first step. I was not the only one." He sets the satchel on the floor. "I should like to hear what Heng has to say."

Jian reaches into his tunic. His fingers close on the folded paper and the drop of black wax, and for one disorienting moment he is not sure it is still there. Then he draws it out and holds it up.

Yan Zhi takes it. He turns it over. He looks at the seal. His fingers, which have not trembled once, tremble just slightly as he breaks the wax.

He reads it standing, with the lamp behind him. It takes him a long time. When he is done he folds it very small and holds it in his closed hand, and does not speak.

"What does it say?" asks Bei.

"That your brother is sorry." The clerk's voice is level. "That he knows what he did. That he gave the boy the key because I once told him that a man is judged by what he does when there is nothing left to gain." He takes off his spectacles and wipes them on his sleeve. "It is a good letter. I wish he had sent it two years ago."

He puts the spectacles back on.

"Now," he says. "The Gate Bearer will wish to know what the Registry is. And I shall tell him. In fifty-three minutes, or less."

* * *

He tells it in order. Jian will remember that afterward, with a kind of numb gratitude: that the man did not skip, did not hedge, did not flinch. He sits on the stool with his hands on his knees and his eyes on the lamp, and speaks in the careful voice of a clerk reading a ledger aloud.

"The Registry has no name," he says. "That is the first thing. It does not call itself the Registry. That is the Sect's word. Inside, it is called the House, or the Office, or nothing at all. Its members do not use names. Each of us is given a number on entry, and our name is burned. I was Seventeen. The man at the next desk was Eighteen. I never learned his true name, though we sat side by side for twenty years."

"Why?"

"So that no name can be taken from the House." The mild eyes flick to him. "You know the line. The Founder's seventh disciple wrote it. The Keeper's house will wear no name. It was a vow, and a practical one. A man with no name cannot be bribed by a family, threatened through a child, or tempted with a seat." He pauses. "It has worked for six hundred years."

"The Seventh Keeper founded it."

"Founded it, yes, in the seventh year after the Founders died. He took the Roll and walked out of the Sect. He built the first House in a cave, with six clerks and a crate of ink. By the end of his life it had forty. By the end of the next century, four hundred." Yan Zhi shrugs. "It grew into the Sect as a vine grows into a wall. A clerk in the Sutra Hall. A deputy in Enforcement. An accountant in the Treasury. The Sect thinks it has one office. It has a thousand desks."

"And its purpose?"

"To keep the record of the Gate." The clerk says it flatly, like a catechism. "That is what we were taught. The Gate opens for a single person, at long intervals, when the Founders' machine calls one. We call such a person an Operator. The House's duty is to find the Operator, to read him, and to decide."

"Decide what?"

"Whether he lives."

The lamp ticks. Bei stirs on her stool but says nothing.

"There have been seven Operators in six centuries," says Yan Zhi. "I know the number because I copied the ledger. The first came in the year after the Founders died. He lasted nine months. The second was a woman, in the fourth century. She went mad. The third and fourth and fifth were killed by the House's hands, in the usual way, quietly, with a clerk's brush and a Blood Shadow. The sixth vanished." He folds his hands. "The seventh was a boy of nine, in the cradle-town of the south, who had the misfortune to be born in a year of famine. He died of a fever, or so the ledger says."

He looks at Jian.

"You are the eighth."

* * *

Jian does not speak for some time.

He is aware of his own heartbeat, steady and slow. The weight of Pebble on his chest. The warmth of the lamp, the smell of coal and stone, the faint ringing of a pick somewhere far above. He is aware that his left arm has begun to ache again, a long dull burn from shoulder to wrist, and that his mouth is dry.

Seven, he thinks. Seven before me. And all but one dead.

"Why?" he says at last. "Why kill them? If the Gate calls an Operator, and the Operator opens it, what is the harm?"

"That is the question I asked." Yan Zhi's mild face does not change. "In my twenty-fifth year, I put it to the Keeper in writing. I was told it was above my number."

"The Keeper."

"The head of the House. I have never seen him. I do not know if he is a man or a woman. All orders come on plum-bark, sealed with a black square, in a hand I have never identified." The clerk's voice drops. "He is called the Keeper of the Roll. And I think, though I cannot prove it, that the Keeper has not been the same person for very long."

"What do you mean?"

"The hand changes. Every thirty or forty years. A different pressure on the brush. A different habit of the d. But the voice does not." He rubs his thumb along the edge of his knee. "The House has said the same thing in the same words since the Seventh Keeper's day. As though a single mind, or a single standing order, had been passed from hand to hand."

"A standing order."

"Yes." Yan Zhi hesitates. It is the first hesitation Jian has seen. "I am going to tell you something, Gate Bearer, that I have never said aloud, and that cost me my number. When I was a young clerk, I found a paper. It was in a ledger I should not have opened. It was the founding charter of the House. It was not in the Seventh Keeper's hand."

"Whose?"

"It was written in a script I could not read. Small, angular, precise. The same script that is cut into the stone of the Dock." The clerk meets his eyes. "And at the bottom, in the Sect's characters, a single line, in the Seventh Keeper's writing. By the instruction of ARK-3."

* * *

The silence that follows is absolute.

Jian lies still. He feels the cold go down his spine, vertebra by vertebra, and settle in his belly like a stone. He is aware that Bei has lifted her head, that her scarred face has gone sharp, that she is looking at him and not at the clerk. He is aware that he has not blinked.

ARK-3.

The signal he saw on the fleet register. The single clean green mark among the dead. The hand that amended his record six hundred and one years ago.

"The Registry," he says slowly, "was founded on the instruction of ARK-3."

"So the charter says."

"It is the hand of ARK-3. In the Sect. In the world."

"I do not know what ARK-3 is." Yan Zhi's voice is quite steady. "I know only that the House has obeyed it for six centuries without ever seeing it. I know that the standing order has never changed. I know that every Operator in my ledger was found, read, and judged within a year of the Gate's call, and that the verdict was always the same, with one exception." He pauses. "Do you know which?"

"The sixth. The one who vanished."

"Yes. The ledger says only: Not found. In a hand that was not the Keeper's." The clerk lifts a thin finger. "The House has been looking for him for two hundred years."

"Why?"

"I do not know." He takes off his spectacles again, and this time his hands do shake. "I know that I spent thirty-one years serving an instruction I did not understand, in the name of a thing I never saw, and that when the Keeper ordered Heng to hold a seven-year-old child on a thread to bring you to heel, I asked, for the second time in my life, why." He puts the glasses back on. "I was told that I had a number, and that it was not Seventeen anymore. I left that night."

"They did not stop you?"

"They did not find me." A faint smile. "I am an excellent clerk. I have always known how to disappear into a ledger."

* * *

"I have one more thing," says Yan Zhi, and for the first time his voice has an edge of weariness, as though he has carried this last piece a long way and is unsure he has the right to set it down.

The pick has fallen silent. The lamp has burned low. Bei has risen and gone to the curtain, where she stands with her broad back to them, listening to the mine. Pebble sleeps on Jian's chest, curled, rising and falling with his breath.

"The question that was put to your mother," the clerk says. "Who was in the room on the night you were born. I wrote it. I wrote it a year ago, on the Keeper's order, and I did not know why."

Jian's hand tightens on the blanket.

"Do you know now?"

"I think so." The mild voice is almost kind. "The House does not ask a question it cannot answer. It asks to see who answers. If your mother had said, no one, she would have been left alone. If she had said, a light, or a voice, or anything that was true, she would have been classed." He pauses. "As a Reader."

"A Reader."

"A person who has seen the Gate's work. It is the House's word for a witness. Readers do not live long." Yan Zhi's eyes are grave. "Your mother has not answered. That is good. It is the only reason she is alive. But the question has been asked, and the House does not let a question go. It will ask again, in a different way. And again." He leans forward. "Every tenth winter the Sect holds the Grand Offering at the Hall of Ancestors, on the solstice. Every disciple attends. Every Elder kneels. The next falls in ten years' time. I have heard, from a man who still sits at a desk, that the Keeper intends to act at that Offering."

"Act how?"

"I do not know. I know only that the word he used was close."

"Close the Gate."

"Or close the Gate Bearer." Yan Zhi spreads his hands. "I do not know which. I do not think the Keeper does either."

* * *

When the clerk has gone, slipping away through the mine's back adit into the dusk, Jian lies a long time in the dark with his eyes open.

Outside, the shadows are gone.

Bei goes up at dusk to look, and comes back with frost on her shoulders and a hard satisfied look on her face. The four hooded watchers on the mine road have withdrawn, she says. All that remains is a ring of trampled snow where they stood, and a single gray thread caught on the thorn of a bush, still faintly twitching. "They know I will not let them in," she says. "They know the miners will not let them in. There are two hundred of us and three hundred picks. Even a Registry has to count."

"Will they come back?"

"Tomorrow. Next week. When you walk out." She hangs the lamp on its nail. "They want you alive, I think. A dead Operator is a thing to be filed. A live one is a question."

"That is a comfort."

"It is not meant to be." But she sits, and hands him the rice, and for a time they eat in a silence that is almost warm.

Bei brings him a second bowl of rice later, and sits beside him again, and says nothing. She is a good silent companion, the kind who knows that a silence need not be filled. After a while he realizes that she is waiting for him to speak.

"I need to go to Red Ridge," he says.

"For the boy."

"For Hui. I have the key. Your brother gave me a deed." He turns his head. "I can walk in three days. I can fight in ten."

"You cannot walk in three days. You can crawl." She says it without unkindness. "Your arm is black to the elbow. You burned the marrow in it. I have seen that once before, in a man who drew on a Spirit Root in winter. He lived. He never lifted a pick again." She looks at him. "What did you do?"

"I tried to draw from a living source. There was none."

"So you drew from yourself."

"Yes."

"Idiot." It is not harsh. It is the plainest word in the world. She takes his left hand in both of hers, turns it over, and looks at the lines on the wrist. The skin is gray as ash. The veins show black under it, and the Spring Vein, which he has carried since the Garden, is a dull scar like a burned rope. "It will not heal this winter. The cold will make it ache. It may not heal at all."

"I know."

"Then why do you go?"

"Because a boy of eight has not spoken in four months," says Lin Jian, "and I told his brother that I would come."

Zhao Bei sets down his hand. For a long moment she regards him, with her small steady eyes the same dark brown as Heng's, and he sees the whole of twenty years go across her face. Then she nods, once, slowly.

"I will go with you," she says. "I have a pick. I am a very bad neighbor."

Behind her, outside the curtain, the mine bell begins to toll the end of the shift. And on his chest, in the dark, the little animal opens one black eye and says, with deep satisfaction:

Good. More friends.
